n:
*Text-critical note:* Codex Leningrad (B19A), on which *BHS* is based, has here “messengers” (הַמַּלְאָכִים, hammalʾakhim), probably as the result of contamination from the occurrence of that word in v. {{2 Samuel 11:4|4}}. The present translation follows most Hebrew mss and the ancient versions, which read “kings” (הַמֶּלָאכִים, hammelakhim).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “go out.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and his servants with him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all Israel.”

*Translator's note:* The disjunctive clause contrasts David’s inactivity with the army’s activity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “on the roof of the house of the king.” So also in vv. {{2 Samuel 11:8|8}}, {{2 Samuel 11:9|9}}.

*Translator's note:* The disjunctive clause highlights this observation and builds the tension of the story.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (the messenger) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and David sent messengers and he took her.”

*Translator's note:* The expression בּוֹא אֶל (boʾ ʾel) means “come to” or “approach,” but is also used as a euphemism for sexual relations, the implied purpose for approaching someone. Here it refers only to the stage of approaching while the next verb describes the result. That she is the subject of this verb (while David is the subject of the next verb) probably indicates that the act was consensual.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he lay down with her.” The verb שָׁכַב (shakav) “to lie down” can be a euphemism for going to bed for sexual relations.

*Translator's note:* The parenthetical disjunctive clause further heightens the tension by letting the reader know that Bathsheba, having just completed her menstrual cycle, is ripe for conception. See P. K. McCarter, *II Samuel* (AB), 286. Since she just had her period, it will also be obvious to those close to the scene that Uriah, who has been away fighting, cannot be the father of the child.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “concerning the peace of Joab and concerning the peace of the people and concerning the peace of the battle.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and wash your feet.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and there went out after him the gift of the king.”
*Text-critical note:* The Lucianic recension of the Old Greek translation lacks the word “all.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lie with.” The verb שָׁכַב (shakav) “to lie down” can be a euphemism for going to bed for sexual relations.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “as you live and as your soul lives.”
*Translator's note:* On the chronology involved here see P. K. McCarter, *II Samuel* (AB), 287.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the valiant men.” This refers in context to the strongest or most valiant defenders of the city Joab and the Israelite army were besieging, so the present translation uses “the best enemy soldiers” for clarity.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “some of the people from the servants of David.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Joab sent and related to David all the matters of the battle.”
*Study note:* The *upper millstone* (*Heb* “millstone of riding”) refers to the heavy circular stone that was commonly rolled over a circular base in order to crush and grind such things as olives.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and came out to us.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “but we were on them.”
*Text-critical note:* The translation follows the *Qere* (“your servants”) rather than the *Kethib* (“your servant”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “let not this matter be evil in your eyes.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “according to this and according to this the sword devours.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “overthrow.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text does not have “with these words.” They are supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “David sent and gathered her to his house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the thing which David had done was evil in the eyes of the Lord.” Note the verbal connection with v. {{2 Samuel 11:25|25}}. Though David did not regard the matter as evil, the Lord certainly did.

*Text-critical note:* A few medieval Hebrew mss, the LXX, and the Syriac Peshitta add “the prophet.” The words are included in a few modern English version (e.g., TEV, CEV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “him”; the referent (David) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Nathan) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text repeats “to him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his sons.”

*Translator's note:* The three Hebrew imperfect verbal forms in this sentence have a customary nuance; they describe past actions that were repeated or typical.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from his morsel.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and on his chest [or perhaps, “lap”] it would lie.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “came to the rich man.” In the translation “arrived at the rich man’s home” has been used for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he refused to take from his flock and from his herd to prepare [a meal] for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who had come to him” (also a second time later in this verse). The word “visit” has been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons and for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and prepared.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the man doing this [is] a son of death.” See {{1 Samuel 20:31|1 Sam 20:31}} for another use of this expression, which must mean “he is as good as dead” or “he deserves to die,” as {{1 Samuel 20:32|1 Sam 20:32}} makes clear.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the lamb he must repay fourfold because he did this thing and because he did not have compassion.”

*Text-critical note:* With the exception of the Lucianic recension, the Old Greek translation has here “sevenfold” rather than “fourfold,” a reading that S. R. Driver thought probably to be the original reading (S. R. Driver, *Notes on the Hebrew Text and the Topography of the Books of Samuel*, 291). However, {{Exodus 22:1|Exod 22:1}} [21:37 HT] specifies fourfold repayment for a stolen sheep, which is consistent with {{2 Samuel 12:6|2 Sam 12:6}}. Some mss of the Targum and the Syriac Peshitta exaggerate the idea to “fortyfold.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the wives of your lord into your chest [or “lap”].” The words “I put” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons and for clarification.

*Translator's note:* Or “word, message.” The “word of the Lord” sometimes refers to a prophetic message from God and sometimes to his past revelation. Here it refers to the Lord’s laws which David has violated.

*Text-critical note:* So the *Qere*; the *Kethib* has “his.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “raise up against you disaster.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “house” (so NAB, NRSV); NCV, TEV, CEV “family.”

*Translator's note:* Or “friend.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will lie down with.” The verb שָׁכַב (shakhav) “to lie down” can be a euphemism for going to bed for sexual relations.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the eyes of this sun.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT has here “because you have caused the enemies of the Lord to treat the Lord with such contempt.” This is one of the so-called tiqqune sopherim, or “emendations of the scribes.” According to this ancient tradition, the scribes changed the text in order to soften somewhat the negative light in which David was presented. If that is the case, the MT reflects the altered text. The present translation departs from the MT here. Elsewhere the Piel stem of this verb means “treat with contempt,” but never “cause someone to treat with contempt.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the Lord struck the child…and he was ill.” It is necessary to repeat “the child” in the translation to make clear who became ill, since “the Lord struck the child that Uriah’s wife had borne to David, and he became very ill” could be understood to mean that David himself became ill.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sought” or “searched for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and David fasted.”

*Translator's note:* The three Hebrew verbs that follow in this verse are perfects with prefixed vav. They may describe repeated past actions or actions which accompanied David’s praying and fasting.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to our voice.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he will do harm.” The object is not stated in the Hebrew text. The statement may be intentionally vague, meaning that he might harm himself or them!
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “David.” The name has been replaced in the translation by the pronoun (“he”) for stylistic reasons.
*Text-critical note:* For the MT בַּעֲבוּר (baʿavur, “for the sake of”) we should probably read בְּעוֹד (beʿod, “while”). See the Lucianic Greek recension, the Syriac Peshitta, and the Targum.

*Translator's note:* The combination of the verb בּוֹא (boʾ; “to come, enter”) and the preposition אֶל (ʾel; “to”) means “to approach, to come to” (HALOT 1:113). This common expression is also used as a euphemism for coming together for sexual relations. Although some take the phrase to be a graphic depiction of a man actions in sexual relations with a woman, certain factors clarify that it is a euphemism. First, the phrase also describes a woman approaching a man for sexual relations ({{2 Samuel 11:4|2 Sam 11:4}}), a situation where this phrase cannot be explicitly descriptive. Second, the phrase is paired here with שָׁכַב (shakhav), “to lie down,” which only makes sense if the two are complementary (compare also {{Genesis 19:33|Gen 19:33-34}} which uses both verbs of Lot’s daughters, but without the preposition). The verb שָׁכַב can imply lying down for sleep or for sexual relations. When בּוֹא אֶל (boʾ ʾel) is used with שָׁכַב (shakhav), they state the natural progression of approaching and then lying with. Hebrew can use the two together, or either separately, as a euphemism for sexual relations. But if the phrase בּוֹא אֶל were already an explicit depiction of sex, then the latter phrase with שָׁכַב, “to lie with,” would be pointless. So {{2 Samuel 11:4|2 Sam 11:4}} and {{2 Samuel 12:24|2 Sam 12:24}} are important evidence for how this phrase really works, and it is appropriate to also use euphemisms in translation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he lay with her.” The phrase is a euphemism for sexual relations.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (David) has been specified in the translation for clarity. While some translations render the pronoun as third person plural (“they”), implying that both David and Bathsheba together named the child, it is likely that the name “Solomon,” which is related to the Hebrew word for “peace” (and may be derived from it) had special significance for David, who would have regarded the birth of a second child to Bathsheba as a confirming sign that God had forgiven his sin and was at peace with him.

*Text-critical note:* The Kethiv reads “he named” while the Qere reads “she named.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “him,” referring to the child.
*Study note:* The name *Jedidiah* means “loved by the Lord.”

*Study note:* Here the narrative resumes the battle story that began in {{2 Samuel 11:1|11:1}} (see {{2 Samuel 11:25|11:25}}). The author has interrupted that story to give the related account of David’s sin with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah. He now returns to the earlier story and brings it to a conclusion.

*Study note:* The expression translated *the water supply of the city* (*Heb* “the city of the waters”) apparently refers to that part of the fortified city that guarded the water supply of the entire city. Joab had already captured this part of the city, but he now defers to King David for the capture of the rest of the city. In this way the king will receive the credit for this achievement.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “people.” So also in vv. {{2 Samuel 12:29|29}}, {{2 Samuel 12:31|31}}.

*Translator's note:* Part of the Greek tradition wrongly understands Hebrew מַלְכָּם (malkam, “their king”) as a proper name (“Milcom”). Some English versions follow the Greek here, rendering the phrase “the crown of Milcom” (so NRSV; cf. also NAB, CEV). TEV takes this as a reference not to the Ammonite king but to “the idol of the Ammonite god Molech.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and its weight [was] a talent of gold.” The weight of this ornamental crown was approximately 75 lbs (34 kg). See P. K. McCarter, *II Samuel* (AB), 313.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “brought out.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to pass through.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and so he would do.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Amnon the son of David loved her.” The following verse indicates the extreme nature of his infatuation, so the translation uses “madly in love” here.

*Study note:* Amnon was the half-brother of Tamar; Absalom was her full blood-brother.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and there was distress to Amnon so that he made himself sick.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he said to him.”

*Translator's note:* A more idiomatic translation might be “Why are you of all people…?”

*Translator's note:* This verb is used in the Hitpael stem only in this chapter of the Hebrew Bible. With the exception of v. {{2 Samuel 13:2|2}} it describes not a real sickness but one pretended in order to entrap Tamar. The Hitpael sometimes, as here, describes the subject making oneself appear to be of a certain character. On this use of the stem, see GKC 149-50 §54.*e*.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from upon me.”

*Text-critical note:* A few medieval Hebrew mss supported by the LXX and Vulgate read the Hiphil וַיּוֹצִיאוּ (vayyotsiʾu) “and they removed everyone,” rather than the MT’s Qal וַיֵּצְאוּ (vayyetseʾu, “they left”). This verb would then match the instructions more closely.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lie with me” (so NAB, NASB, NRSV); NCV “come and have sexual relations with me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and you will be like one of the fools.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Now.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to her voice.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he humiliated her and lay with her.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Amnon hated her with very great hatred.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for greater was the hatred with which he hated her than the love with which he loved her.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “No, because this great evil is [worse] than the other which you did with me, by sending me away.” Perhaps the broken syntax reflects her hysteria and outrage.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “send this [one] from upon me to the outside.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew expression used here (כְּתֹנֶת פַּסִּים, ketonet passim) is found only here and in {{Genesis 37:3|Gen 37:3}}, {{Genesis 37:23|23}}, {{Genesis 37:32|32}}. Hebrew פַּס (pas) can refer to the palm of the hand or the sole of the foot; here the idea is probably that of a long robe reaching to the feet and having sleeves reaching to the wrists. The notion of a “coat of many colors” (KJV, ASV “garment of divers colors”), a familiar translation for the phrase in Genesis, is based primarily on the translation adopted in the LXX χιτῶνα ποικίλον (chitōna poikilon) and does not have a great deal of support.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his”; the referent (Amnon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb is a perfect with nonconsecutive vav, probably indicating an action (locking the door) that complements the preceding one (pushing her out the door).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Don’t set your heart to this thing!” Elsewhere this phrase means to disregard or not pay attention to something (e.g. {{Exodus 7:23|Exod 7:23}}). It is a callous thing to say to Tamar, but to the degree that what he said becomes known, it misleads people from understanding that he is personally plotting revenge ({{2 Samuel 13:22|13:22}}, {{2 Samuel 13:28|28}}).

*Text-critical note:* The LXX and part of the Old Latin tradition include the following addition to v. {{2 Samuel 13:21|21}}, also included in some English versions (e.g., NAB, NRSV, CEV): “But he did not grieve the spirit of Amnon his son, because he loved him, since he was his firstborn.” Note David’s attitude toward his son Adonijah in {{1 Kings 1:6|1 Kgs 1:6}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your servant has sheepshearers.” The phrase “your servant” also occurs at the end of the verse and is translated as "me".

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Absalom) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Text-critical note:* Here and in v. {{2 Samuel 13:27|27}} the translation follows 4QSama ויפצר (vayyiftsar, “and he pressed”) rather than the MT וַיִּפְרָץ (vayyifrats, “and he broke through”). This emended reading seems also to underlie the translations of the LXX (καὶ ἐβιάσατο, kai ebiasato), the Syriac Peshitta (weʾalseh), and Vulgate (*cogeret eum*).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (the king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (David) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when good is the heart of Amnon with wine.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and become sons of valor.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it was placed on the mouth of Absalom.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Amnon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they lifted their voice and wept.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with a great weeping.”
*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text leaves the word “David” to be inferred. The Syriac Peshitta and Vulgate add the word “David.” Most of the Greek tradition includes the words “King David” here.

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows 4QSama in reading רוּחַ הַמֶּלֶךְ (ruakh hammelekh, “the spirit of the king”) rather than the MT דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ (david hammelekh, “David the king”). The understanding reflected in the translation above is that David, though alienated during this time from his son Absalom, still had an abiding love and concern for him. He longed for reconciliation with him. A rather different interpretation of the verse supposes that David’s interest in taking military action against Absalom grew slack with the passing of time, and this in turn enabled David’s advisers to encourage him toward reconciliation with Absalom. For the latter view, see P. K. McCarter, *II Samuel* (AB), 344, and cf. CEV.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “was consoled over Amnon because he was dead.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the heart of the king was upon.” The Syriac Peshitta adds the verb ʾethreʿi (“was reconciled”).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew Hitpael verbal form here indicates pretended rather than genuine action.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “these many days.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “put the words in her mouth” (so NASB, NIV).

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows many medieval Hebrew mss in reading וַתַּבֹא (vattavoʾ, “and she went”) rather than the MT וַתֹּאמֶר (vattoʾmer, “and she said”). The MT reading shows confusion with וַתֹּאמֶר later in the verse. The emendation suggested here is supported by the LXX, the Syriac Peshitta, some mss of the Targum, and Vulgate.

*Translator's note:* The word “me” is left to be inferred in the Hebrew text; it is present in the Syriac Peshitta and Vulgate.

*Translator's note:* Here and elsewhere (vv. {{2 Samuel 14:7|7}}, {{2 Samuel 14:12|12}}, {{2 Samuel 14:15|15a}}, {{2 Samuel 14:17|17}}, {{2 Samuel 14:19|19}}) the woman uses a term which suggests a lower level female servant. She uses the term to express her humility before the king. However, she uses a different term in vv. {{2 Samuel 14:15|15b-16}}. See the note at v. {{2 Samuel 14:15|15}} for a discussion of the rhetorical purpose of this switch in terminology.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in exchange for the life.” The Hebrew preposition ב (bet, “in”) here is the so-called bet pretii, or bet (ב) of price, defining the value attached to someone or something.

*Study note:* *My remaining coal* is here metaphorical language, describing the one remaining son as her only source of lingering hope for continuing the family line.

*Translator's note:* The words “in that case” are not in the Hebrew text, but may be inferred from the context. They are supplied in the translation for the sake of clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “let the king remember.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “of your son.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he devises plans for the one banished from him not to be banished.”

*Text-critical note:* The LXX (ὄψεταί με, opsetai me) has misunderstood the Hebrew יֵרְאֻנִי (yereʾuni, Piel perfect, “they have made me fearful”), taking the verb to be a form of the verb רָאָה (raʾah, “to see”) rather than the verb יָרֵא (yareʾ, “to fear”). The fact that the Greek translators were working with an unvocalized Hebrew text (i.e., consonants only) made them very susceptible to this type of error.

*Translator's note:* Here and in v. {{2 Samuel 14:16|16}} the woman refers to herself as the king’s אָמָה (ʾamah), a term that refers to a higher level female servant toward whom the master might have some obligation. Like the other term, this word expresses her humility, but it also suggests that the king might have some obligation to treat her in accordance with the principles of justice.

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Translator's note:* Or “will.” The imperfect verbal form can have either an indicative or modal nuance. The use of “perhaps” in v. {{2 Samuel 14:15|15b}} suggests the latter here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in order to deliver his maid.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “destroy.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the inheritance of God.” The expression refers to the property that was granted to her family line in the division of the land authorized by God.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to know all that is in the land.”
*Text-critical note:* Many medieval Hebrew mss have “you” rather than “I.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “blessed.”

*Text-critical note:* The present translation reads with the *Qere* “your” rather than the MT “his.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Like Absalom there was not a handsome man in all Israel to boast exceedingly.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there was not in him a blemish.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for it was heavy upon him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “two hundred shekels.” The modern equivalent would be about three pounds (1.4 kg).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and there were born.”

*Text-critical note:* The LXX adds here the following words: “And she became a wife to Rehoboam the son of Solomon and bore to him Abia.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Joab) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Text-critical note:* The LXX adds here the following words: “And the servants of Absalom burned them up. And the servants of Joab came to him, rending their garments. They said….”

*Translator's note:* The word “Joab’s” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he.” Joab, acting on behalf of the king, may be the implied subject.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Absalom) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Absalom.” For stylistic reasons the name has been replaced by the pronoun (“him”) in the translation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “acquired for himself.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to run ahead of him.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your servant.” So also in vv. {{2 Samuel 15:8|8}}, {{2 Samuel 15:15|15}}, {{2 Samuel 15:21|21}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Who will make me?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a complaint and a judgment.” The expression is a hendiadys.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Absalom) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Text-critical note:* The MT has here “forty,” but this is presumably a scribal error for “four.” The context will not tolerate a period of forty years prior to the rebellion of Absalom. The Lucianic Greek recension (τέσσαρα ἔτη, tessara etē), the Syriac Peshitta (ʾarbaʿ sanin), and Vulgate (*post quattuor autem annos*) in fact have the expected reading “four years.” Most English translations follow the versions in reading “four” here, although some (e.g. KJV, ASV, NASB, NKJV), following the MT, read “forty.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for your servant vowed a vow.” The formal court style of referring to one’s self in third person (“your servant”) has been translated here as first person for clarity.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Absalom) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “being invited and going naively and they did not know anything.”

*Translator's note:* Traditionally, “counselor,” but this term is more often associated with psychological counseling today, so “adviser” was used in the translation instead.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, the adviser of David, from his city, from Giloh, while he was sacrificing.” It is not entirely clear who (Absalom or Ahithophel) was offering the sacrifices.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the heart of the men of Israel is with Absalom.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Arise!”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “let’s flee.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “thrust.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and strike the city with the edge of the sword.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “according to all that my lord the king will choose, behold your servants!”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and all his house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “women, concubines.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “crossing over near his hand.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “crossing over near the face of.”

*Translator's note:* The word “new” is not in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation to make it clear that David refers to Absalom, not himself.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “place.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “brothers,” but see v. {{2 Samuel 15:22|22}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “loyal love and truth.” The expression is a hendiadys.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “be with.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Come and cross over.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “crossed over.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the little ones.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with a great voice.”

Literally the Hebrew text says “he took three spears in his hand and thrust them into the *heart* of Absalom while he was still alive in the *heart* of the oak tree.” This figure of speech involves the use of the same word in different senses and is known as antanaclasis. *Study note:* The significance of the statement *it fell out* here is unclear. If the dagger fell out of its sheath before Joab got to Amasa, how then did he kill him? Josephus, *Ant*. 7.11.7 (7.284), suggested that as Joab approached Amasa he deliberately caused the dagger to fall to the ground at an opportune moment as though by accident. When he bent over and picked it up, he then stabbed Amasa with it. Others have tried to make a case for thinking that two swords are referred to—the one that fell out and another that Joab kept concealed until the last moment. But nothing in the text clearly supports this view. Perhaps Josephus’ understanding is best, but it is by no means obvious in the text either.
